DynaCrys: Crystal Generation with Dynamic Space-Group Diffusion

Zhuotao Jin Affiliation: NVIDIA Affiliation: Center for Computational Science and Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University    Xiaoyun Wang Affiliation: NVIDIA    Nicholas Brawand Affiliation: The MITRE Corporation    Roman Zubatyuk Affiliation: NVIDIA    Atul Thakur Affiliation: NVIDIA    Eric Qu Affiliation: NVIDIA Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley    Boris Kozinsky Affiliation: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University Affiliation: Robert Bosch Research and Technology Center    Justin Smith Affiliation: NVIDIA
Abstract

The search for new crystalline materials spans an enormous compositional and structural space. Generating candidates in this space requires jointly modeling discrete crystallographic symmetry, elemental composition, and continuous geometry. We introduce DynaCrys, a generative model for crystals in which the space group co-evolves with Wyckoff occupations and elements through a coupled symbolic diffusion process. The structured space-group transitions follow crystallographic group–subgroup relations. As the space group changes, a shared, pretrained symmetry codebook provides both the legality-constrained stochastic decoder and the symmetry-constrained crystal-geometry model with a common representation of the corresponding Wyckoff vocabulary. Across large-scale evaluations using two independent relaxation-and-evaluation engines, DynaCrys achieves best-in-class performance in symmetry-aware discovery of stable, unique, and novel crystals, both overall and under the additional requirement of nontrivial post-relaxation symmetry. It also enables fast sampling while generating structures with consistently low relaxation-induced structural displacements.

1 Introduction

Discovering functional inorganic materials requires searching an enormous space for crystals that are both novel and thermodynamically promising. Deep generative models have emerged as a way to propose such candidates directly (Xie et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2024; Zeni et al., 2025). Crystals, however, are not unconstrained point clouds: a space group GG specifies the admissible Wyckoff positions, their multiplicities, and their coordinate degrees of freedom (Aroyo, 2016). A crystal generator must therefore couple a discrete symmetry description to the continuous geometry it constrains.

In the explicit-GG generation procedures reviewed in Section 2, the space group is fixed before subsequent crystal variables are generated conditionally on it. Because GG determines the admissible Wyckoff vocabulary and possible orbit decompositions (Aroyo, 2016), this conditioning keeps subsequent variables compatible with the initial GG, but does not allow GG itself to be revised as generation proceeds.

We introduce DynaCrys, a two-stage crystal generator that keeps GG inside the evolving generative state. Its symbolic diffusion stage jointly updates the space group, Wyckoff occupations, and chemical elements along the reverse trajectory. Each occupation selects one space-group-specific Wyckoff row and an element, leaving the row’s remaining free coordinates to be generated during the geometry stage. The space-group corruption kernel incorporates crystallographic group–subgroup relations underlying Bärnighausen trees (Bärnighausen, 1980), while a pretrained symmetry codebook shared by the symbolic and geometry stages provides a common representation for the space-group-dependent Wyckoff vocabularies.

The symbolic process alternates legality-constrained decoding with re-noising until it reaches a final clean protostructure. A separate symmetry-constrained geometry stage then uses this protostructure to generate the lattice and free Wyckoff coordinates while enforcing the symmetry constraints encoded by the decoded space group throughout sampling (Section 4; Figure 1).

To compare these methods on a common basis, we apply the same protocol for relaxation and analysis to approximately 10,000 candidates per method and independently repeat the complete evaluation with a second MLIP. This large candidate count reduces finite-sample variation, while consistent downstream settings limit differences caused by evaluation choices (Section 5.1).

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Dynamic space-group diffusion. We introduce a coupled symbolic diffusion process that treats the space group itself as a diffusion variable that can be revised jointly with Wyckoff occupations and elements throughout the reverse process. The space-group corruption kernel incorporates crystallographic group–subgroup relations.

  • •

    A legal symbolic-to-geometric interface. We develop a crystal-specific legality-constrained decoder whose accepted samples follow the model distribution conditioned on crystallographic legality, without evaluating its global constrained normalizer. We then couple each decoded protostructure to a symmetry-constrained geometry diffusion model through the shared symmetry codebook.

  • •

    Empirical validation. Across two independent relaxation-and-evaluation engines and a same-machine timing comparison, DynaCrys shows consistently strong performance across discovery metrics, energetic stability, relaxation-induced structural displacement, and sampling efficiency.

2 Related Work

Crystal generators without an explicit space-group variable.

CDVAE, DiffCSP, FlowMM, and MatterGen (Xie et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2024; Zeni et al., 2025) generate lattices, fractional coordinates, and compositions with no space-group variable in the generative state; crystallographic symmetry is therefore an a posteriori property of the generated coordinates rather than an explicit sampled state.

Symmetry-aware, static-GG generators.

A second family makes the space group explicit but fixes it before generating subsequent crystal variables (Levy et al., 2025; Ekström Kelvinius et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2025; Ruple et al., 2026; Chang et al., 2026; Kazeev et al., 2025; Jiao et al., 2024). Whether sampled or supplied externally, the group conditions the remainder of the generation process and is not revised thereafter. In DynaCrys, GG is instead part of the diffusion state and can be revised jointly with Wyckoff occupations and elements throughout the reverse process.

Symmetry representations.

SymmCD (Levy et al., 2025) encodes site symmetries as binary operation–axis descriptors, WyckoffDiff (Ekström Kelvinius et al., 2025) represents Wyckoff occupations with space-group-specific discrete variables, and SGEquiDiff (Chang et al., 2025) uses predefined crystallographic features for space groups and Wyckoff positions. DynaCrys instead learns a shared codebook of continuous embeddings from operation-based descriptors of space groups and Wyckoff rows. The row embeddings parameterize both the continuous corruption channel and space-group-conditional row prediction for the vocabulary associated with each GtG_{t} (Section 4.2).

Constrained sampling in diffusion models.

Existing approaches to constrained or conditional diffusion sampling include iterative projection (Christopher et al., 2024), discrete-state guidance (Nisonoff et al., 2025), and sequential Monte Carlo (Wu et al., 2023). DynaCrys instead enforces symbolic legality by rejection sampling over its finite symbolic state space. Conditional on acceptance, the decoder samples exactly from the denoiser’s factorized clean-state distribution conditioned on legality, without evaluating the global constrained normalizer (Section 4.3).

3 Space Groups and Wyckoff Orbits

A periodic crystal consists of a lattice basis L∈ℝ3×3L\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} and atoms in one unit cell, represented here by fractional coordinates 𝐱∈[0,1)3\mathbf{x}\in[0,1)^{3}. Rather than treating these atoms as independent points, a space group GG organizes them into symmetry orbits. There are 230 three-dimensional space-group types (Aroyo, 2016). Each operation g=(Rg,𝐭g)g=(R_{g},\mathbf{t}_{g}) acts on fractional coordinates as g⋅𝐱=(Rg​𝐱+𝐭g)mod1g\cdot\mathbf{x}=(R_{g}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{t}_{g})\bmod 1. The orbit of a representative coordinate is the set of distinct symmetry-equivalent sites obtained by applying all operations in GG.

A Wyckoff position, represented here by a row r∈ℛGr\in\mathcal{R}_{G} of the space-group table, describes a family of such orbits. The row specifies an orbit multiplicity μG,r\mu_{G,r} and the number of coordinates dofG,r\operatorname{dof}_{G,r} left free by symmetry. Choosing those coordinates fixes one particular orbit from the family. In a label such as 4​e4e, the numeral gives the orbit multiplicity, while the letter is a conventional identifier local to that space group and distinguishes Wyckoff positions (Aroyo, 2016). A symbolic orbit occupation selects a row and an element ZZ but leaves the free coordinates unspecified; multiple occupations may use the same row. Once its coordinates are chosen, ZZ is placed on all μG,r\mu_{G,r} sites of the resulting orbit. A collection of orbit occupations therefore determines the crystal’s symbolic symmetry and composition, while the lattice parameters and free coordinates remain to be generated as continuous geometry (Figure 2a).

The vocabulary ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G} is specific to the space group. Wyckoff letters are labels local to each space group, and changing GG changes the available rows, their multiplicities, and their free-coordinate parameterizations. Group–subgroup relations organize these changes (Figure 2c). A maximal relation connects two space groups with no intermediate space group. Every such step is either translationengleiche (tt), which preserves the translation lattice while reducing point group symmetry, or klassengleiche (kk), which retains the point group while reducing translational symmetry (Aroyo, 2016). Restricting GG to a subgroup HH can split one GG-orbit into several independently parameterized HH-orbits (Figure 2b). In the illustrated P​m→P​1Pm\rightarrow P1 example, the orbit occupying the P​mPm row 1​b1b becomes one occupation of the P​1P1 row 1​a1a, while the orbit occupying the P​mPm row 2​c2c splits into two P​1P1 1​a1a occupations. Once the mirror constraint is removed, the three resulting representative coordinates may vary independently.

Consequently, revising the space group during symbolic generation does more than update a categorical label: it changes the admissible orbit representation and the continuous degrees of freedom available to the subsequent geometry stage. Section 4 therefore treats GG, the orbit occupations, and their elements as coupled components of one evolving symbolic state.

4 Dynamic Space-Group Crystal Generation

DynaCrys separates crystal generation into two stages. A symbolic diffusion model first samples a protostructure containing the space group, Wyckoff-row occupations, and their elements. Conditioned on this discrete state, a symmetry-constrained geometry model then generates the lattice and the free coordinates that instantiate the complete crystal.

4.1 Protostructure state and shared symmetry representation

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} denote the space-group vocabulary supported by the model. A protostructure PP (Goodall et al., 2022) is

P=(G,K,{(Zi,ri)}i=1K),P=\bigl(G,\;K,\;\{(Z_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{K}\bigr), (1)

where G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G} is the space group, KK is the number of orbit occupations, ri∈ℛGr_{i}\in\mathcal{R}_{G} is a Wyckoff row, and ZiZ_{i} is the element assigned to that occupation. The occupations form an unordered multiset, the same row may occur more than once, and PP contains neither a lattice nor free coordinates.

The symbolic diffusion represents PP with a fixed-width padded clean state x0x_{0}. At noise level tt, the corresponding state is

xt=(Gt,Kt,{(mi,t,Zi,t,yi,t)}i=1M).x_{t}=\bigl(G_{t},\;K_{t},\;\{(m_{i,t},Z_{i,t},y_{i,t})\}_{i=1}^{M}\bigr). (2)

Here mi,tm_{i,t} marks an active or padded slot, Zi,tZ_{i,t} is the corresponding element or padding symbol, and yi,t∈ℝdy_{i,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a noisy Wyckoff-row vector. At t=0t=0, the active slots encode the occupations of PP and the remaining slots are padding. The noisy state xtx_{t} need not decode directly to a legal protostructure.

Because the row vocabulary ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G} depends on GG, DynaCrys represents space groups and Wyckoff rows with a shared symmetry codebook containing vectors cGc_{G} and cG,rc_{G,r}. The codebook is pretrained from crystallographic descriptors. Its row vectors serve as the clean centers of the continuous row channel and as the tied vectors of the space-group-conditional row head. The geometry model also receives the space-group and row codebook embeddings as conditioning features. At each diffusion step, cGtc_{G_{t}} represents the current noisy space group GtG_{t}. The shared codebook therefore provides a common representation of space-group-specific Wyckoff vocabularies across the symbolic and geometry stages. Appendix C provides details of the codebook construction.

4.2 Coupled symbolic diffusion

Forward corruption.

The symbolic forward process is a diffusion process defined by a family of marginal kernels qt​(xt∣x0)q_{t}(x_{t}\mid x_{0}) (Austin et al., 2021). Its space-group channel mixes a structured transition with a reset to the training distribution:

qtG​(Gt∣G0)=λt​Rt​(Gt∣G0)+(1−λt)​πG​(Gt).q_{t}^{G}(G_{t}\mid G_{0})=\lambda_{t}R_{t}(G_{t}\mid G_{0})+(1-\lambda_{t})\pi_{G}(G_{t}). (3)

The transition RtR_{t} diffuses over the undirected graph induced by maximal translationengleiche and klassengleiche group–subgroup relations on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. This graph supplies the transition geometry of the space-group corruption; the reset component makes the terminal distribution independent of G0G_{0}.

After drawing GtG_{t}, the forward process samples KtK_{t} and partitions the MM slots into survivors, births, and padding. Survivors retain a corrupted signal from distinct clean occupations, whereas birth rows are drawn from the vocabulary of the current GtG_{t}; the row vectors and elements are then corrupted conditionally on this partition. This construction accommodates a changing number of occupations and defines the same marginal kernel for training-time corruption and sampling-time re-noising. Further details on the channel distributions and noise schedules are provided in Appendix B.

Set denoising network.

The denoiser represents xtx_{t} by one global token for (Gt,Kt,t)(G_{t},K_{t},t) and MM orbit-slot tokens containing (mi,t,Zi,t,yi,t)(m_{i,t},Z_{i,t},y_{i,t}). A Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017) processes these tokens without slot positional encodings, making its slot outputs permutation equivariant. Global and slot-wise heads predict the clean state as

pθ(G0∣xt),pθ(K0∣xt),{piact(⋅∣xt),pi(r∣G,xt),pi(Z∣G,r,xt)}i=1M.p_{\theta}(G_{0}\mid x_{t}),\qquad p_{\theta}(K_{0}\mid x_{t}),\qquad\left\{p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}(\,\cdot\mid x_{t}),\;p_{i}(r\mid G,x_{t}),\;p_{i}(Z\mid G,r,x_{t})\right\}_{i=1}^{M}. (4)

Here pθ​(G0∣xt)p_{\theta}(G_{0}\mid x_{t}) and pθ​(K0∣xt)p_{\theta}(K_{0}\mid x_{t}) are the global predictions of the clean space group and orbit count. For slot ii, piactp_{i}^{\mathrm{act}} is the binary active-state distribution: values 11 and 00 denote an occupied and padded slot, respectively. The row head pi​(r∣G,xt)p_{i}(r\mid G,x_{t}) assigns probability only to valid rows r∈ℛGr\in\mathcal{R}_{G} and uses their shared-codebook vectors as classifier weights. The element head pi​(Z∣G,r,xt)p_{i}(Z\mid G,r,x_{t}) predicts the element.

Training objective.

The symbolic model predicts x0x_{0} with the set objective

ℒsym=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}={} ℒG+wK​ℒK+wm​ℒmask+wr​ℒr+wZ​ℒZ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{G}+w_{K}\mathcal{L}_{K}+w_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+w_{r}\mathcal{L}_{r}+w_{Z}\mathcal{L}_{Z} (5)
+saux​(wcap​ℒcap+wN​ℒN+wcomp​ℒcomp).\displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{aux}}\left(w_{\mathrm{cap}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}+w_{N}\mathcal{L}_{N}+w_{\mathrm{comp}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}\right).

Here ℒG\mathcal{L}_{G} and ℒK\mathcal{L}_{K} are cross-entropies for the global space-group and orbit-count predictions. We first use a Hungarian assignment (Carion et al., 2020) to match the MM predicted slots to the K0K_{0} clean occupations and M−K0M-K_{0} padding targets. Writing π⁡(j)\pi(j) for the predicted slot matched to target jj, and 𝔖M\mathfrak{S}_{M} for the set of permutations of the MM slots, the optimal assignment is

π⋆=arg⁡minπ∈𝔖M​[∑j=1K0Cocc​(π⁡(j),j)+∑j=K0+1MCpad​(π⁡(j))],\displaystyle\pi^{\star}=\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{M}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{K_{0}}C_{\mathrm{occ}}\bigl(\pi(j),j\bigr)+\sum_{j=K_{0}+1}^{M}C_{\mathrm{pad}}\bigl(\pi(j)\bigr)\right], (6)
Cocc​(i,j)=−wm​log​piact​(1∣xt)−wr​log​pi​(rj∣G0,xt)−wZ​log​pi​(Zj∣G0,rj,xt),\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{occ}}(i,j)=-w_{m}\log p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}(1\mid x_{t})-w_{r}\log p_{i}(r_{j}\mid G_{0},x_{t})-w_{Z}\log p_{i}(Z_{j}\mid G_{0},r_{j},x_{t}),
Cpad​(i)=−wm​log⁡piact​(0∣xt).\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{pad}}(i)=-w_{m}\log p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}(0\mid x_{t}).

Here CoccC_{\mathrm{occ}} is the cost of assigning a predicted slot to a clean occupation, whereas CpadC_{\mathrm{pad}} is the cost of assigning it to a padding target. After matching, ℒmask\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}} is the active-state binary cross-entropy over all matched slots, while ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} and ℒZ\mathcal{L}_{Z} are the row and element negative log-likelihoods over the occupied matches. Among the auxiliary terms, ℒcap\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}} penalizes excess expected row occupancy, while ℒN\mathcal{L}_{N} and ℒcomp\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}} match the expected conventional-cell atom count and composition to the clean target. The sampler separately enforces row-capacity limits and the fixed atom-count cap. The row-conditioned element head is refined with an additional identity regularizer. Further details on the prediction heads, assignment costs, loss terms, and optimization settings are provided in Appendix D.

4.3 Legality-constrained reverse sampling

The heads in Eq. (4) define a factorized clean-state distribution, but their independent predictions need not jointly satisfy the model’s symbolic legality constraints. Let 𝒳legal\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}} denote the corresponding legal set: GG must lie in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, exactly KK slots must be active, every selected row must belong to ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G}, and the collection of occupations must satisfy the row-capacity and atom-count constraints. The stochastic decoder targets the factorized distribution conditioned on this set,

p~θ(x0∣xt)∝pθfac(x0∣xt)𝟏[x0∈𝒳legal].\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\propto p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\mathbf{1}[x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}]. (7)

Here pθfacp_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}} is the factorized distribution induced by the heads in Eq. (4), 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the legality indicator, and p~θ\widetilde{p}_{\theta} is the resulting distribution restricted to and renormalized over 𝒳legal\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}.

Direct normalization of Eq. (7) over 𝒳legal\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}} would require summing over a combinatorial number of legal symbolic states. Instead, let aia_{i} be the active logit of slot ii, let ωi=exp⁡(ai)\omega_{i}=\exp(a_{i}), and define the elementary symmetric polynomial

eK​(𝝎)=∑A⊆{1,…,M}|A|=K∏i∈Aωi.e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\\ |A|=K\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i}.

After drawing GG, the decoder samples the orbit count KK and active-slot set AA according to

qprop​(K∣xt)∝pθ​(K0=K∣xt)​eK​(𝝎),\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{prop}}(K\mid x_{t})\propto p_{\theta}(K_{0}=K\mid x_{t})e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega}), (8)
qprop​(A∣K,xt)=∏i∈AωieK​(𝝎)(|A|=K).\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{prop}}(A\mid K,x_{t})=\frac{\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i}}{e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega})}\qquad(|A|=K).

The eKe_{K} factors cancel when the two proposal distributions are multiplied. After sampling GG, KK, the active set, and the selected rows, the decoder rejects skeletons that violate these constraints and draws their elements after acceptance.

Proposition 1.

Conditional on acceptance, the stochastic decoder returns an exact draw from p~θ(⋅∣xt)\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}) without evaluating its global normalizer.

Appendix E gives the derivation and complete sampling procedure. Reverse generation repeatedly predicts a legal clean state and then applies the same marginal forward kernel at the next lower noise level:

x^0(t)∼p~θ(⋅∣xt),xt−1∼qt−1(⋅∣x^0(t))(t>0).\hat{x}_{0}^{(t)}\sim\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad x_{t-1}\sim q_{t-1}(\cdot\mid\hat{x}_{0}^{(t)})\quad(t>0). (9)

At t=0t=0, removing inactive slots from x^0(0)\hat{x}_{0}^{(0)} and disregarding slot order yields the final protostructure PP. The space group is thus resampled jointly with the other symbolic variables throughout the reverse trajectory rather than fixed in advance.

4.4 Symmetry-constrained geometry generation

The final protostructure PP specifies the space group, Wyckoff occupations, and composition. The geometry stage generates a lattice compatible with the crystal family of GG and the free fractional coordinates of one representative point, or orbit anchor, per occupied orbit.

Geometry denoising.

Building on the continuous diffusion framework of DiffCSP++ (Jiao et al., 2024), an atom-level message-passing network operates on the full conventional cell reconstructed from the occupied orbit anchors and is conditioned on PP, the diffusion time, and the shared symmetry codebook. Let btb_{t} denote the noisy lattice representation and XtX_{t} the noisy full-cell fractional coordinates. The two heads minimize

ℒlat=𝔼[‖ϵG−ϵ^θ(bt,Xt,P,t)‖22],ϵG=ΠGlinϵ,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert\epsilon_{G}-\widehat{\epsilon}_{\theta}(b_{t},X_{t},P,t)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right],\qquad\epsilon_{G}=\Pi_{G}^{\mathrm{lin}}\epsilon, (10)
ℒcoord=𝔼⁡[‖Π𝒜⁡(P)​(u^θ​(Xt,bt,P,t)−uwn∗​(Xt,X0,σt))‖22].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coord}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert\Pi_{\mathcal{A}(P)}\!\left(\widehat{u}_{\theta}(X_{t},b_{t},P,t)-u_{\mathrm{wn}}^{*}(X_{t},X_{0};\sigma_{t})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right].

Here ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) is standard Gaussian lattice noise, ϵG=ΠGlin​ϵ\epsilon_{G}=\Pi_{G}^{\mathrm{lin}}\epsilon is its projection onto the crystal-family subspace, and ϵ^θ\widehat{\epsilon}_{\theta} is the lattice-noise prediction. The clean full-cell fractional coordinates are denoted by X0X_{0}, σt\sigma_{t} is the coordinate-noise scale, and uwn∗u_{\mathrm{wn}}^{*} is the wrapped-normal denoising target. The coordinate head predicts the denoising field u^θ\widehat{u}_{\theta}. Finally, Π𝒜⁡(P)\Pi_{\mathcal{A}(P)} projects a full-cell coordinate field onto 𝒜⁡(P)\mathcal{A}(P), the free degrees of freedom of the orbit anchors specified by PP.

Symmetry-constrained sampling.

At every reverse step, the lattice representation is projected to the subspace compatible with the crystal family of GG. The anchor coordinates are updated only along their allowed degrees of freedom and expanded through the corresponding Wyckoff operations into complete atomic orbits. By construction, every intermediate geometry is invariant under the operations of the decoded space group GG. Further details on the lattice representation, geometry objectives, and reverse sampling procedure are provided in Appendix F.

5 Evaluation

5.1 Evaluation setup

We evaluate unconditional crystal generation on MP-20 (Xie et al., 2022). Its training partition is used to train DynaCrys and as the reference set for novelty. Each evaluated set contains approximately 10,000 candidates. Using relatively large and similar generation budgets reduces finite-sample variation.

Generated structures are relaxed and then evaluated for energy above the convex hull, novelty with respect to the training partition, uniqueness within the generated set, and post-relaxation space-group symmetry. We apply the same relaxation, hull, structure-matching, and symmetry-analysis settings to all available methods so that differences in these downstream choices do not obscure the comparison. CHGNet (Deng et al., 2023) provides the primary relaxation endpoint, and we independently repeat the complete relaxation and analysis pipeline using MACE-MP-0 (Batatia et al., 2025). The two engines are treated as separate evaluation rulers.

Following the criterion used by MatterGen (Zeni et al., 2025), we define the stable–unique–novel rate, SUN@τ\tau, as the fraction of generated candidates that are stable at threshold τ\tau (ehull≤τe_{\mathrm{hull}}\leq\tau), unique, and novel. SSUN@τ\tau additionally requires the relaxed structure to exhibit nontrivial (non-P​1P1) space-group symmetry. We report the strict threshold τ=0\tau=0 and the metastable threshold τ=0.1\tau=0.1 eV/atom. Space groups used for the main SSUN comparison are identified at symprec=0.1=0.1 Å. Full metric definitions and denominator conventions are given in Appendix G.

We compare with DiffCSP (Jiao et al., 2023), MatterGen (Zeni et al., 2025), FlowMM (Miller et al., 2024), DiffCSP++ (Jiao et al., 2024), SymmCD (Levy et al., 2025), WyFormer (Kazeev et al., 2025), and SGEquiDiff (Chang et al., 2025). Publicly released samples are used when available; SGEquiDiff is sampled from its released checkpoint. All baseline values in this comparison are obtained under the common evaluation protocol.

For readability, Table 1 separates the evaluated generators by whether they explicitly represent crystallographic symmetry. Generators in the second block use a space group, Wyckoff description, or crystallographic template; those in the first do not.

5.2 Stable, symmetric, and novel material discovery

The core comparison reports SUN and SSUN at both stability thresholds together with the median relaxed ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}}. Reporting both stability thresholds separates the strict-stability candidates from the broader metastable regime; the median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}} characterizes the typical energetic quality of the relaxed population. The canonical DynaCrys configuration is the reference model throughout the paper; DynaCrys-B and DynaCrys-C share its architecture and differ only in the row-capacity rule and symbolic training schedule specified in Appendix D.4.

Across both evaluation engines, all three DynaCrys configurations outperform every baseline on SUN@0 and SSUN@0, and occupy the top three positions in the explicit-symmetry block on SUN@0.1 and SSUN@0.1. All three configurations also have lower median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}} than every explicit-symmetry baseline under both engines, while DynaCrys-C ranks first overall.

To test whether DynaCrys uses the evolving symbolic state when updating the space group, we replace the learned proposal for GG at every reverse step with the empirical space-group marginal of the training set, leaving the rest of the sampler unchanged. For the canonical configuration, SUN@0 falls from 9.28%9.28\% to 3.01%3.01\% with the generation seed held fixed. This degradation supports conditioning the space-group proposal on the evolving symbolic state. Results across all three configurations are reported in Appendix K.

5.3 Sample quality and relaxed stability

We complement the SUN and SSUN rates with standard crystal-generation proxy metrics (Xie et al., 2022): structural and compositional validity, coverage recall and precision, distributional distances for density and the number of distinct elements, the Template U.N. rate in crystallographic-template space, the effective number of generated space groups NeffG=exp(−∑gpglogpg)N_{\mathrm{eff}}^{G}=\exp(-\sum_{g}p_{g}\log p_{g}) (Betala et al., 2025), and relaxed stability. Together, these quantities check whether strong discovery performance is accompanied by chemically valid samples, broad coverage of the reference distribution, diverse crystallographic templates and space groups, and favorable relaxed energies.

Overall, the DynaCrys models combine strong sample quality with leading relaxed stability. Table 2 shows that structural validity and coverage are near saturation across the comparison. All three DynaCrys configurations exceed every baseline on strict relaxed stability, while DynaCrys-C ranks second overall at the metastable threshold. The canonical DynaCrys configuration attains a lower density-distribution distance than every baseline except DiffCSP++ (Jiao et al., 2024), which uses fixed crystallographic templates sampled from the training set, and a lower element-count distance than every baseline except WyFormer. DynaCrys-C attains the lowest element-count distance overall. The joint discovery gains in Table 1 are accompanied by high relaxed stability and near-saturated structural validity and coverage. The DynaCrys models also remain competitive in compositional validity, distributional agreement, and crystallographic-template discovery.

5.4 Relaxation-induced structural displacement

The preceding metrics characterize discovery and sample quality, but not how far a generated geometry moves during relaxation. We therefore compare each as-generated structure with its independently relaxed endpoint under both evaluation engines. This analysis characterizes the geometric response to relaxation and is kept separate from the discovery table so that energetic quality and structural displacement are not conflated.

In Table 3, all three DynaCrys models achieve lower mean RMSD than every baseline except MatterGen while maintaining high matched-pair rates, indicating that their generated structures remain comparatively close to the relaxed endpoints.

5.5 Quality–efficiency trade-off

Same-machine sampling times are available for SGEquiDiff, SymmCD, WyFormer, DynaCrys, and DynaCrys-small. The canonical DynaCrys configuration serves as the quality reference, whereas DynaCrys-small uses a smaller hidden dimension and fewer layers in the crystal-geometry model while retaining the same symbolic generator.

Reducing the size of the crystal-geometry model makes DynaCrys-small 1.59×1.59\times faster while retaining close SUN and SSUN values at both stability thresholds. DynaCrys-small exceeds every baseline in this comparison on all four SUN/SSUN columns while maintaining a low median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}}.

The sensitivity of the SUN rates to the number of geometry reverse steps is reported in Appendix J.

6 Limitations and Conclusion

Limitations.

As in prior computational crystal-generation work, our stability assessments rely on computational screening proxies. In our evaluation, hull distances are referenced to a finite snapshot of known structures. A low ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}} does not by itself imply that a structure can be synthesized experimentally. The models in this comparison represent infinite, fully ordered crystals at zero temperature; defects, disorder, and finite-temperature effects lie outside the modeled scope.

Conclusion.

DynaCrys makes the space group part of the evolving generative state, allowing it to be revised jointly with Wyckoff occupations and elements throughout symbolic generation. A legality-constrained stochastic decoder connects this state to a symmetry-constrained crystal-geometry model. Across both evaluation engines, the DynaCrys models lead symmetry-aware generators in stable–unique–novel discovery, both overall and under the additional requirement of nontrivial post-relaxation symmetry. They also enable fast sampling while generating structures with consistently low relaxation-induced structural displacements. Together, these results demonstrate that dynamic space-group diffusion provides an effective foundation for symmetry-aware crystal generation.

Appendix A Symbolic State Space and Legality

This appendix defines the finite state space of the symbolic model and the legal clean states used by the decoder.

A.1 Symbolic state space

Let

𝒢={G:nGtrain>0}\mathcal{G}=\{G:n_{G}^{\mathrm{train}}>0\}

be the model vocabulary of 168 training-supported space groups. Using PyXtal’s space group and Wyckoff position tables (Fredericks et al., 2021), we construct the crystallographic row catalogue and associated symmetry operations for all 230 space groups, with ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G} denoting the valid Wyckoff rows of group GG. Across this catalogue there are 1,731 valid (G,r)(G,r) pairs, and the row table for each space group is padded to width 27.

The symbolic state uses M=20M=20 orbit slots. A clean state has

G∈𝒢,K∈{1,…,M},∑i=1Mmi=K.G\in\mathcal{G},\qquad K\in\{1,\ldots,M\},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{M}m_{i}=K.

Each active slot has ri∈ℛGr_{i}\in\mathcal{R}_{G} and carries a categorical element label Zi∈𝒵Z_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}, while inactive slots use separate PAD symbols. Noisy states replace the row index by the continuous row vector yiy_{i} defined in Appendix B.

A.2 Crystallographic tables

The symbolic and geometry stages share the following crystallographic metadata for each valid (G,r)(G,r):

Symbol Meaning
μG,r\mu_{G,r} multiplicity in the conventional cell
dofG,r\operatorname{dof}_{G,r} number of free anchor coordinates
sG,rs_{G,r} site-symmetry label
eG,re_{G,r} enumeration within (G,sG,r)(G,s_{G,r})

The valid-row mask restricts every space-group-conditional row distribution to ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G}. Multiplicity enters the atom-count constraint, while the remaining metadata parameterize the shared symmetry codebook and the geometry model. The configuration-specific capacity uG,ru_{G,r} is defined below.

A.3 Capacity and legal clean states

For the canonical DynaCrys configuration, let q0.99train​(G,r)q_{0.99}^{\mathrm{train}}(G,r) be the 99th percentile of the within-structure repetition count of row (G,r)(G,r), computed on the training partition. Let bG,r=⌊Nmax/μG,r⌋b_{G,r}=\lfloor N_{\max}/\mu_{G,r}\rfloor be the largest occupation compatible with a cap of Nmax=80N_{\max}=80 atoms in the conventional cell. The resulting capacity is

uG,r={0,r∉ℛG,1,dofG,r=0​ or ​q0.99train​(G,r)​ is unavailable,max⁡{1,min⁡(⌈q0.99train​(G,r)⌉,bG,r)},otherwise.u_{G,r}=\begin{cases}0,&r\notin\mathcal{R}_{G},\\ 1,&\operatorname{dof}_{G,r}=0\text{ or }q_{0.99}^{\mathrm{train}}(G,r)\text{ is unavailable},\\ \displaystyle\max\!\left\{1,\,\min\!\left(\left\lceil q_{0.99}^{\mathrm{train}}(G,r)\right\rceil,\,b_{G,r}\right)\right\},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (11)

The alternative reported configurations use the multiplicity-based capacity rule in Appendix D.4; Table 5 records the configuration differences.

Write a padded clean state as x0=(G,K,A,R,Z)x_{0}=(G,K,A,R,Z), where A⊆{1,…,M}A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\} is the active-slot set and R=(ri)i∈AR=(r_{i})_{i\in A}, Z=(Zi)i∈AZ=(Z_{i})_{i\in A}. Define the number of active occupations assigned to row rr by

nr(A,R)=∑i∈A𝟏[ri=r].n_{r}(A,R)=\sum_{i\in A}\mathbf{1}[r_{i}=r].

For a chosen capacity table uu, the legal clean-state set in Eq. (7) is

𝒳legal≡𝒳legal​(u)={(G,K,A,R,Z):G∈𝒢,|A|=K,(ri,Zi)∈ℛG×𝒵∀i∈A,nr​(A,R)≤uG,r∀r∈ℛG,∑i∈AμG,ri≤Nmax}.\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}\equiv\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}(u)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &(G,K,A,R,Z):\quad G\in\mathcal{G},\quad|A|=K,\\ &(r_{i},Z_{i})\in\mathcal{R}_{G}\times\mathcal{Z}\quad\forall i\in A,\\ &n_{r}(A,R)\leq u_{G,r}\quad\forall r\in\mathcal{R}_{G},\\ &\displaystyle\sum_{i\in A}\mu_{G,r_{i}}\leq N_{\max}\end{aligned}\right\}. (12)

Appendix B Forward Corruption Kernels

The symbolic forward process is a family of marginal kernels qt​(xt∣x0)q_{t}(x_{t}\mid x_{0}). At each noise level it samples

Gt⟶Kt⟶survivor–birth–PAD partition⟶{(mi,t,Zi,t,yi,t)}i=1M.G_{t}\longrightarrow K_{t}\longrightarrow\text{survivor--birth--PAD partition}\longrightarrow\{(m_{i,t},Z_{i,t},y_{i,t})\}_{i=1}^{M}.

The same family is used for training-time corruption and reverse-time re-noising.

B.1 Training priors

All reset and birth distributions are estimated on the training partition. Writing nGn_{G}, nG,rn_{G,r}, and nZn_{Z} for the corresponding counts,

πG​(G)=nG∑G′∈𝒢nG′,πZ​(Z)=nZ∑Z′∈𝒵nZ′.\pi_{G}(G)=\frac{n_{G}}{\sum_{G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}}n_{G^{\prime}}},\qquad\pi_{Z}(Z)=\frac{n_{Z}}{\sum_{Z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}}n_{Z^{\prime}}}. (13)

The row prior is smoothed within the valid vocabulary of each group:

πR​(r∣G)=nG,r+1∑r′∈ℛG(nG,r′+1),r∈ℛG.\pi_{R}(r\mid G)=\frac{n_{G,r}+1}{\sum_{r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{G}}(n_{G,r^{\prime}}+1)},\qquad r\in\mathcal{R}_{G}. (14)

For the orbit count, let p^train​(K∣G)\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{train}}(K\mid G) and p^train​(K)\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{train}}(K) be the space-group-conditional and global empirical distributions. We use

πK​(K∣G)=(1−ρG)​p^train​(K∣G)+ρG​p^train​(K),ρG=αKnG+αK,αK=20.\pi_{K}(K\mid G)=(1-\rho_{G})\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{train}}(K\mid G)+\rho_{G}\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{train}}(K),\qquad\rho_{G}=\frac{\alpha_{K}}{n_{G}+\alpha_{K}},\quad\alpha_{K}=20. (15)

Here αK=20\alpha_{K}=20 is a smoothing pseudo-count controlling shrinkage toward the global orbit-count distribution.

B.2 Space-group graph and kernel

The graph on 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains the maximal translationengleiche and klassengleiche group–subgroup relations, with edge directions removed and self-relations omitted. Let AA be its adjacency matrix, A~=A+I\widetilde{A}=A+I, D=diag⁡(A~​𝟏)D=\operatorname{diag}(\widetilde{A}\mathbf{1}), and

W𝒢=D−1​A~,Q=W𝒢−I,Rs=exp⁡(βmax​s​Q),βmax=4,W_{\mathcal{G}}=D^{-1}\widetilde{A},\qquad Q=W_{\mathcal{G}}-I,\qquad R_{s}=\exp\!\left(\beta_{\max}sQ\right),\quad\beta_{\max}=4, (16)

qtG​(Gt∣G0)=λG​(s)​Rs​(Gt∣G0)+[1−λG​(s)]​πG​(Gt).q_{t}^{G}(G_{t}\mid G_{0})=\lambda_{G}(s)R_{s}(G_{t}\mid G_{0})+\bigl[1-\lambda_{G}(s)\bigr]\pi_{G}(G_{t}). (17)

Given the sampled group, the orbit count follows

qtK​(Kt∣K0,Gt)=λK​(s)​δK0​(Kt)+[1−λK​(s)]​πK​(Kt∣Gt).q_{t}^{K}(K_{t}\mid K_{0},G_{t})=\lambda_{K}(s)\delta_{K_{0}}(K_{t})+\bigl[1-\lambda_{K}(s)\bigr]\pi_{K}(K_{t}\mid G_{t}). (18)

The number of surviving clean occupations is

St∼Binomial⁡(min⁡(K0,Kt),αS​(s)).S_{t}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(\min(K_{0},K_{t}),\,\alpha_{S}(s)\right). (19)

The StS_{t} survivors are matched to distinct clean occupations sampled uniformly without replacement. Together with Kt−StK_{t}-S_{t} births, they are placed uniformly among the MM slots; the remaining slots are PAD.

Let cG,rc_{G,r} and cpadc_{\mathrm{pad}} be the row and padding vectors of the shared codebook in Appendix C. For each slot,

yi,t=μi,t+σy​(s)​ϵi,ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),y_{i,t}=\mu_{i,t}+\sigma_{y}(s)\epsilon_{i},\qquad\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), (20)

with

μi,t={α¯y​(s)​cG0,ri0,survivor matched to ​ri0,cGt,ribirth,ribirth∼πR(⋅∣Gt),birth,cpad,PAD.\mu_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)}\,c_{G_{0},r_{i}^{0}},&\text{survivor matched to }r_{i}^{0},\\ c_{G_{t},r_{i}^{\mathrm{birth}}},\quad r_{i}^{\mathrm{birth}}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid G_{t}),&\text{birth},\\ c_{\mathrm{pad}},&\text{PAD}.\end{cases} (21)

qtZ​(Zi,t∣Zi0)=αZ​(s)​δZi0​(Zi,t)+[1−αZ​(s)]​πZ​(Zi,t).q_{t}^{Z}(Z_{i,t}\mid Z_{i}^{0})=\alpha_{Z}(s)\delta_{Z_{i}^{0}}(Z_{i,t})+\bigl[1-\alpha_{Z}(s)\bigr]\pi_{Z}(Z_{i,t}). (22)

B.4 Schedules and terminal prior

The discrete channels share a quadratic retention schedule, and the row channel uses a cosine signal schedule:

λG​(s)=λK​(s)=αS​(s)=αZ​(s)=(1−s)2,\displaystyle\lambda_{G}(s)=\lambda_{K}(s)=\alpha_{S}(s)=\alpha_{Z}(s)=(1-s)^{2}, (23)
α¯y(s)=cos2(π​s2),σy(s)=1−α¯y​(s).\displaystyle\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)=\cos^{2}\!\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right),\qquad\sigma_{y}(s)=\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)}.

Here α¯y​(s)\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s) is the retained row-signal power and σy​(s)\sigma_{y}(s) is the row-noise scale. The training horizon is T=1000T=1000; at generation time, the reverse sampler operates at 200 noise levels arranged in descending order along this schedule.

At s=1s=1, all clean-state retention terms vanish. The terminal state can therefore be sampled directly as

GT∼πG,KT∼πK(⋅∣GT),AT∼Unif{A⊆{1,…,M}:|A|=KT},\displaystyle G_{T}\sim\pi_{G},\qquad K_{T}\sim\pi_{K}(\cdot\mid G_{T}),\qquad A_{T}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}:|A|=K_{T}\}, (24)
ri,T∼πR(⋅∣GT),Zi,T∼πZ,yi,T=cGT,ri,T+ϵi(i∈AT).\displaystyle r_{i,T}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid G_{T}),\qquad Z_{i,T}\sim\pi_{Z},\qquad y_{i,T}=c_{G_{T},r_{i,T}}+\epsilon_{i}\quad(i\in A_{T}).

Here mi,T=𝟏[i∈AT]m_{i,T}=\mathbf{1}[i\in A_{T}]. On PAD slots, yi,T=cpad+ϵiy_{i,T}=c_{\mathrm{pad}}+\epsilon_{i}, and Zi,TZ_{i,T} is the element PAD symbol. This distribution contains no dependence on x0x_{0} and is the starting distribution of the reverse sampler.

Appendix C Shared Symmetry Codebook

The codebook maps space groups and space-group-specific Wyckoff rows into a common vector space. It is constructed once, frozen, and shared by the symbolic and geometry stages.

C.1 Space-group and row representations

For a symmetry operation g=(R∣τ)g=(R\mid\tau) in the fractional-coordinate basis, define

ϕ⁡(g)=[vec⁡(R),τmod1,detR,tr⁡R]∈ℝ14.\phi(g)=\left[\operatorname{vec}(R),\,\tau\bmod 1,\,\det R,\,\operatorname{tr}R\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{14}. (25)

A shared operation encoder eϕe_{\phi} maps these features to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let SGS_{G} denote the operation set of space group GG. A learned map fGf_{G} produces the space-group embedding from the pooled operation features:

cG=fG​[meang∈SG⁡eϕ​(g)∥maxg∈SG⁡eϕ​(g)].c_{G}=f_{G}\!\left[\operatorname{mean}_{g\in S_{G}}e_{\phi}(g)\;\middle\|\;\operatorname{max}_{g\in S_{G}}e_{\phi}(g)\right]. (26)

For row rr, let 𝒞G,r\mathcal{C}_{G,r} be its orbit-generating coset representatives and ℋG,r\mathcal{H}_{G,r} the stabilizer of its representative. A learned map fRf_{R} produces the row embedding from the space-group embedding, operation-derived features, and row metadata:

cG,r=fR[\displaystyle c_{G,r}=f_{R}\Big[ cG,meang∈𝒞G,r⁡eϕ​(g),meang∈ℋG,r⁡eϕ​(g),\displaystyle c_{G},\,\operatorname{mean}_{g\in\mathcal{C}_{G,r}}e_{\phi}(g),\,\operatorname{mean}_{g\in\mathcal{H}_{G,r}}e_{\phi}(g), (27)
emb(μG,r),emb(dofG,r),emb(sG,r),emb(eG,r)].\displaystyle\operatorname{emb}(\mu_{G,r}),\,\operatorname{emb}(\operatorname{dof}_{G,r}),\,\operatorname{emb}(s_{G,r}),\,\operatorname{emb}(e_{G,r})\Big].

Here eG,re_{G,r} enumerates rows within the same (G,site-symmetry)(G,\text{site-symmetry}) class. The codebook width is d=128d=128, and each metadata embedding has width 16. A separately initialized cpadc_{\mathrm{pad}} represents padded rows.

C.2 Pretraining and freezing

Pretraining has two stages. The first fits deterministic crystallographic labels from operation-derived representations. From cGc_{G}, the model predicts the space-group type, crystal system, centering, and point group; an operation-only row representation predicts the number of free coordinates and the site-symmetry label. The sum of these cross-entropies is denoted by ℒstruct\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{struct}}.

The second stage freezes the symmetry-operation encoder and the space-group encoder and refines the modules that construct the row embeddings. A row center is corrupted with the row-channel cosine schedule in Eq. (23),

c~G,r=α¯y​(s)​cG,r+1−α¯y​(s)​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),\widetilde{c}_{G,r}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)}\,c_{G,r}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)}\,\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),

and retrieved among the valid rows of the same group with a cosine-softmax loss

ℒretr=−log⁡exp⁡(cos⁡(c~G,r,cG,r)/τretr)∑r′∈ℛGexp⁡(cos⁡(c~G,r,cG,r′)/τretr),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retr}}=-\log\frac{\exp\!\left(\cos(\widetilde{c}_{G,r},c_{G,r})/\tau_{\mathrm{retr}}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{G}}\exp\!\left(\cos(\widetilde{c}_{G,r},c_{G,r^{\prime}})/\tau_{\mathrm{retr}}\right)},

where τretr\tau_{\mathrm{retr}} is the retrieval temperature. Distinct rows within a group are separated by

ℒsep=meanG,r≠r′r,r′∈ℛG​[ReLU⁡(cos⁡(cG,r,cG,r′)−m)]2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}=\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}G,\ r\neq r^{\prime}\\ r,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{G}\end{subarray}}{\operatorname{mean}}\left[\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\cos(c_{G,r},c_{G,r^{\prime}})-m\right)\right]^{2}. (28)

The second-stage objective is

ℒcb=ℒretr+λsep​ℒsep.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cb}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retr}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}. (29)

The shared training settings are summarized below.

Setting Value
operation / codebook width 128 / 128
metadata width 16
steps per stage 3,000
optimizer AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with cosine decay
learning rate 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}
stage-1 / stage-2 weight decay 0 / 0.01
retrieval temperature / noise draws 0.1 / 4
separation margin mm / weight λsep\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}} 0.5 / 1

After training, every nonzero vector is normalized as

c←d​c∥c∥2,c\leftarrow\sqrt{d}\,\frac{c}{\lVert c\rVert_{2}}, (30)

so each vector has unit root-mean-square coordinate magnitude. The resulting cGc_{G}, cG,rc_{G,r}, and cpadc_{\mathrm{pad}} tables are frozen.

C.3 Use in DynaCrys

The frozen cGtc_{G_{t}} represents the current noisy space group in the symbolic denoiser. The row vectors cG,rc_{G,r} serve both as centers of the continuous row channel and as the tied vectors of the space-group-conditional row head. The accepted cGc_{G} and cG,rc_{G,r} also condition the geometry model. The three reported DynaCrys configurations and their geometry stage use the same frozen codebook.

Appendix D Symbolic Denoiser and Training

This appendix specifies the set denoiser, its prediction heads, and the objective summarized in Section 4.2.

D.1 Permutation-equivariant set denoiser

The noisy state is encoded as one global token and MM orbit-slot tokens:

hglobalin=MLP⁡[cGt,eKt,et],hiin=MLP⁡[emi,eZi,yi,et,cGt].h_{\mathrm{global}}^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left[c_{G_{t}},e_{K_{t}},e_{t}\right],\qquad h_{i}^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left[e_{m_{i}},e_{Z_{i}},y_{i},e_{t},c_{G_{t}}\right]. (31)

Here ete_{t} is a sinusoidal time embedding passed through an MLP. A Transformer encoder processes the tokens without slot positional encodings. Its slot outputs are therefore equivariant to permutations of the orbit occupations, while the global output is invariant to those permutations.

Linear heads on the global output predict G0G_{0} and K0K_{0}. A slot-wise active head predicts whether each output corresponds to an occupied orbit or padding. The remaining slot heads predict its Wyckoff row and element.

D.2 Row and element heads

For a candidate space group GG, the row head classifies only over ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G}. Its logits are tied to the shared codebook with RMS normalization (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019):

ℓi,r(G)=q^i⊤​c^G,rτ+bG,r,\displaystyle\ell_{i,r}^{(G)}=\frac{\widehat{q}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{c}_{G,r}}{\tau}+b_{G,r}, (32)
q^i=normalize⁡(RMSNorm⁡(Wq​hi)+gy​(t)​λy​RMSNorm⁡(yi)),\displaystyle\widehat{q}_{i}=\operatorname{normalize}\!\left(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(W_{q}h_{i})+g_{y}(t)\lambda_{y}\operatorname{RMSNorm}(y_{i})\right),

where c^G,r=normalize⁡(cG,r)\widehat{c}_{G,r}=\operatorname{normalize}(c_{G,r}), τ\tau and λy\lambda_{y} are learned scalars, bG,rb_{G,r} is a row bias, s=t/Ts=t/T, and gy​(t)=α¯y​(s)g_{y}(t)=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{y}(s)}. The invalid-row logits are masked before the row-wise softmax. During training, the clean space group G0G_{0} determines the row vocabulary ℛG0\mathcal{R}_{G_{0}}; during sampling, the row head is evaluated over ℛG\mathcal{R}_{G} for each proposed clean space group GG.

The element head conditions its logits on the selected (G,r)(G,r) through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) (Perez et al., 2018):

ℓiZ​(G,r)=[1+γraw​(cG,r)]⊙WZ​hi+β⁡(cG,r),\ell_{i}^{Z}(G,r)=\left[1+\gamma_{\mathrm{raw}}(c_{G,r})\right]\odot W_{Z}h_{i}+\beta(c_{G,r}), (33)

where a shared MLP produces γraw\gamma_{\mathrm{raw}} and β\beta from the row code. The modulation is initialized at the identity. Its regularizer is

ℒFiLM=λFiLM​1|𝒵|​mean(G,r)​valid​(∥γraw​(cG,r)∥22+∥β⁡(cG,r)∥22).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FiLM}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{FiLM}}\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Z}|}\underset{(G,r)\ \mathrm{valid}}{\operatorname{mean}}\left(\lVert\gamma_{\mathrm{raw}}(c_{G,r})\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert\beta(c_{G,r})\rVert_{2}^{2}\right). (34)

Here |𝒵||\mathcal{Z}| is the element vocabulary size.

D.3 Set objective and assignment

The clean-state prediction loss is

ℒsym=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}={} ℒG+wK​ℒK+wm​ℒmask+wr​ℒr+wZ​ℒZ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{G}+w_{K}\mathcal{L}_{K}+w_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+w_{r}\mathcal{L}_{r}+w_{Z}\mathcal{L}_{Z} (35)
+saux​(wcap​ℒcap+wN​ℒN+wcomp​ℒcomp).\displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{aux}}\left(w_{\mathrm{cap}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}+w_{N}\mathcal{L}_{N}+w_{\mathrm{comp}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}\right).

The global losses are the clean-target cross-entropies ℒG=−log⁡pθ​(G0∣xt)\mathcal{L}_{G}=-\log p_{\theta}(G_{0}\mid x_{t}) and ℒK=−log⁡pθ​(K0∣xt)\mathcal{L}_{K}=-\log p_{\theta}(K_{0}\mid x_{t}) for the predicted space-group and orbit-count distributions, respectively. For the slot losses, a Hungarian assignment aligns the MM predictions with the K0K_{0} clean occupations and M−K0M-K_{0} padding targets. The assignment cost is

Cocc​(i,j)=−wm​log⁡σ⁡(ai)−wr​log​pi​(rj∣G0)−wZ​log​pi​(Zj∣G0,rj),\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{occ}}(i,j)=-w_{m}\log\sigma(a_{i})-w_{r}\log p_{i}(r_{j}\mid G_{0})-w_{Z}\log p_{i}(Z_{j}\mid G_{0},r_{j}), (36)
Cpad​(i)=−wm​log⁡(1−σ⁡(ai)).\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{pad}}(i)=-w_{m}\log\!\left(1-\sigma(a_{i})\right).

After assignment, ℒmask\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}} is the binary cross-entropy between each slot’s active-state prediction and its matched target. The losses ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} and ℒZ\mathcal{L}_{Z} are cross-entropies between the predicted row and element distributions and their respective clean targets over the matched occupied slots.

The auxiliary losses are computed from the expected row occupations n^r=∑ipiact​pi​(r∣G0)\widehat{n}_{r}=\sum_{i}p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}p_{i}(r\mid G_{0}):

ℒcap=∑rReLU⁡(n^r−uG0,r)2,ℒN=(N^−Nsym,0)2,whereN^=∑ipiact​∑rpi​(r∣G0)​μG0,r.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}=\sum_{r}\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\widehat{n}_{r}-u_{G_{0},r}\right)^{2},\\ &\mathcal{L}_{N}=(\widehat{N}-N_{\mathrm{sym},0})^{2},\\ &\text{where}\quad\widehat{N}=\sum_{i}p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}\sum_{r}p_{i}(r\mid G_{0})\mu_{G_{0},r}.\end{aligned} (37)
ℒcomp=∑a(C^a−C0,a)2,whereC^a=∑ipiact​∑rpi​(r∣G0)​μG0,r​pi​(a∣G0,r).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}=\sum_{a}(\widehat{C}_{a}-C_{0,a})^{2},\\ &\text{where}\quad\widehat{C}_{a}=\sum_{i}p_{i}^{\mathrm{act}}\sum_{r}p_{i}(r\mid G_{0})\mu_{G_{0},r}p_{i}(a\mid G_{0},r).\end{aligned} (38)

Here uG0,ru_{G_{0},r} is the permitted occupation count, μG0,r\mu_{G_{0},r} is the Wyckoff multiplicity, and N^\widehat{N} and Nsym,0N_{\mathrm{sym},0} are the expected and clean conventional-cell atom counts, respectively. Likewise, C^a\widehat{C}_{a} and C0,aC_{0,a} are the expected and clean multiplicity-weighted counts of element aa. The decoder in Appendix E separately enforces the row-capacity limits and its fixed atom-count cap.

D.4 Training settings

The symbolic denoiser is trained with Eq. (35). The row-conditioned element head is then refined while all other parameters are frozen, using

ℒrefine=ℒsym+ℒFiLM.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{refine}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sym}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FiLM}}. (39)

The reported configurations differ only in their capacity rule and symbolic training schedule. Under the multiplicity-based rule, a valid row has capacity

uG,rmult={1,dofG,r=0,max⁡{1,⌊Nmax/μG,r⌋},dofG,r>0.u_{G,r}^{\mathrm{mult}}=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{dof}_{G,r}=0,\\ \max\!\left\{1,\left\lfloor N_{\max}/\mu_{G,r}\right\rfloor\right\},&\operatorname{dof}_{G,r}>0.\end{cases}

Appendix E Legality-Constrained Decoding

E.1 Constrained target

Fix a noisy state xtx_{t}, and abbreviate the denoiser outputs in Eq. (4) as pG​(G)p_{G}(G), pK​(K)p_{K}(K), active probabilities πi\pi_{i}, row distributions pi​(r∣G)p_{i}(r\mid G), and element conditionals pi​(Z∣G,r)p_{i}(Z\mid G,r). For a clean symbolic state x0=(G,K,A,𝐫,𝐙)x_{0}=(G,K,A,\mathbf{r},\mathbf{Z}) with active-slot set A⊆{1,…,M}A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}, the factorized joint distribution is

pθfac​(x0∣xt)=pG​(G)​pK​(K)​∏i∈Aπi​pi​(ri∣G)​pi​(Zi∣G,ri)​∏i∉A(1−πi).p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})=p_{G}(G)\,p_{K}(K)\prod_{i\in A}\pi_{i}\,p_{i}(r_{i}\mid G)\,p_{i}(Z_{i}\mid G,r_{i})\prod_{i\notin A}(1-\pi_{i}). (40)

Its joint score is Sθ​(x0∣xt)=log⁡pθfac​(x0∣xt)S_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})=\log p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}}(x_{0}\mid x_{t}). Given the legal set 𝒳legal\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}} from Section 4.3, the stochastic decoder targets the constrained distribution

p~θ​(x0∣xt)=pθfac(x0∣xt)𝟏[x0∈𝒳legal]∑x∈𝒳legalpθfac​(x∣xt).\widetilde{p}_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})=\frac{p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\mathbf{1}[x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}]}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}}}p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{fac}}(x\mid x_{t})}. (41)

For the decoder comparison, we use a constrained maximum a posteriori (MAP) comparator that retains the top five candidates under pGp_{G} and pKp_{K}, respectively, and performs deterministic constrained search over the resulting GG–KK pairs.

E.2 Elementary-symmetric stochastic proposal

Write ωi=πi/(1−πi)=exp⁡(ai)\omega_{i}=\pi_{i}/(1-\pi_{i})=\exp(a_{i}), where aia_{i} is the active logit. The elementary symmetric polynomial

ek​(𝝎)=∑A⊆{1,…,M}|A|=k∏i∈Aωie_{k}(\boldsymbol{\omega})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\\ |A|=k\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i} (42)

normalizes the distribution over size-kk active sets. It is evaluated by the recursion

Fi​(k)=Fi+1​(k)+ωi​Fi+1​(k−1),FM+1​(0)=1,FM+1​(k>0)=0,F_{i}(k)=F_{i+1}(k)+\omega_{i}F_{i+1}(k-1),\qquad F_{M+1}(0)=1,\quad F_{M+1}(k>0)=0, (43)

for which F1​(k)=ek​(𝝎)F_{1}(k)=e_{k}(\boldsymbol{\omega}). The same table gives the conditional inclusion probability

Pr⁡(i∈A∣k​ active slots remain)=ωi​Fi+1​(k−1)Fi​(k).\Pr(i\in A\mid k\text{ active slots remain})=\frac{\omega_{i}F_{i+1}(k-1)}{F_{i}(k)}. (44)

The proposal draws G∼pGG\sim p_{G}, draws KK with probability proportional to pK​(K)​eK​(𝝎)p_{K}(K)e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega}), draws AA from

q⁡(A∣K)=∏i∈AωieK​(𝝎)for |A|=K,q(A\mid K)=\frac{\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i}}{e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega})}\quad\text{for }|A|=K, (45)

and then draws each ri∼pi(⋅∣G)r_{i}\sim p_{i}(\cdot\mid G).

E.3 Exactness

We prove Proposition 1. Let s=(G,K,A,𝐫)s=(G,K,A,\mathbf{r}) denote the symbolic skeleton, and let 𝒮legal\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}} be the projection of 𝒳legal\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{legal}} onto these variables. Because ∑Z∈𝒵pi​(Z∣G,ri)=1\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{i}(Z\mid G,r_{i})=1 for every occupied slot, marginalizing Eq. (40) over 𝐙\mathbf{Z} gives

pθskel​(s∣xt)=c0​pG​(G)​pK​(K)​∏i∈Aωi​pi​(ri∣G),c0=∏i=1M(1−πi).p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{skel}}(s\mid x_{t})=c_{0}\,p_{G}(G)\,p_{K}(K)\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i}\,p_{i}(r_{i}\mid G),\qquad c_{0}=\prod_{i=1}^{M}(1-\pi_{i}). (46)

Let ZK=∑kpK​(k)​ek​(𝝎)Z_{K}=\sum_{k}p_{K}(k)e_{k}(\boldsymbol{\omega}). One proposal attempt has density

q⁡(s)\displaystyle q(s) =pG​(G)​pK​(K)​eK​(𝝎)ZK​∏i∈AωieK​(𝝎)​∏i∈Api​(ri∣G)\displaystyle=p_{G}(G)\frac{p_{K}(K)e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega})}{Z_{K}}\frac{\prod_{i\in A}\omega_{i}}{e_{K}(\boldsymbol{\omega})}\prod_{i\in A}p_{i}(r_{i}\mid G)
=pθskel​(s∣xt)ZK​c0.\displaystyle=\frac{p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{skel}}(s\mid x_{t})}{Z_{K}c_{0}}. (47)

The elementary-symmetric factors therefore cancel, and the proposal is proportional to the unconstrained skeleton marginal. Conditioning an attempt on s∈𝒮legals\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}} cancels the remaining constant:

Pr⁡(s∣s∈𝒮legal)=pθskel(s∣xt)𝟏[s∈𝒮legal]∑s′∈𝒮legalpθskel​(s′∣xt).\Pr(s\mid s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}})=\frac{p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{skel}}(s\mid x_{t})\mathbf{1}[s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}}]}{\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}}}p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{skel}}(s^{\prime}\mid x_{t})}. (48)

After acceptance, drawing each element from pi(⋅∣G,ri)p_{i}(\cdot\mid G,r_{i}) restores the full joint distribution in Eq. (41). Thus the accepted output is an exact sample from the constrained target without evaluating its global normalizer.

E.4 Sampling procedure

For each reverse step, the elementary-symmetric table is computed once. For at most RR attempts, the decoder draws (G,K,A,𝐫)(G,K,A,\mathbf{r}) from the proposal above and checks whether the resulting skeleton lies in 𝒮legal\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{legal}}. On acceptance, it draws 𝐙\mathbf{Z} from the element conditionals and returns the complete clean symbolic state; otherwise it redraws the entire skeleton. If none of the RR attempts is accepted, the decoder reports a rejection to the reverse sampler.

E.5 Decoder comparison

Table 7 compares the two decoders using the same trained symbolic checkpoint. Stochastic constrained decoding gives higher uniqueness and novelty, as well as higher SUN rates at both stability thresholds. Constrained MAP instead gives higher RelStab at both thresholds and a lower median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}}. This pattern reflects a mode-seeking trade-off: constrained MAP concentrates outputs in a more stable region, whereas stochastic decoding retains higher uniqueness and novelty and yields higher SUN rates.

Appendix F Symmetry-Constrained Geometry Generation

The geometry model receives an accepted protostructure P=(G,K,{(Zi,ri)}i=1K)P=(G,K,\{(Z_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{K}) from the symbolic stage and generates a lattice together with the free fractional coordinates of its occupied Wyckoff orbits. Its symmetry-constrained diffusion of the lattice representation and orbit-anchor coordinates builds on DiffCSP++ (Jiao et al., 2024). Here GG determines the lattice subspace, each rir_{i} determines the orbit chart and expansion operators, and the denoiser receives the corresponding element and shared-codebook embeddings.

F.1 Geometry denoiser

The denoiser is an atom-level message-passing network over the expanded unit cell. Periodicity enters through Fourier features of fractional-coordinate differences and the current lattice representation. The network also receives the diffusion time and protostructure conditioning. It produces a coordinate denoising field for every atom and a pooled lattice-noise prediction.

F.2 Lattice diffusion under crystal-family constraints

Let b∈ℝ6b\in\mathbb{R}^{6} be the coordinates of log⁡L​L⊤\log\sqrt{LL^{\top}} in an orthonormal basis for symmetric matrices. This rotation-invariant representation is projected onto the crystal-family subspace associated with GG by the affine map ΠG​(b)=ΠGlin​b+dG\Pi_{G}(b)=\Pi_{G}^{\mathrm{lin}}b+d_{G}. The forward process is

bt=ΠG​(α¯t​b0+1−α¯t​ϵ),ϵG=ΠGlin​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I),b_{t}=\Pi_{G}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,b_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon\right),\qquad\epsilon_{G}=\Pi_{G}^{\mathrm{lin}}\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), (49)

and the lattice head minimizes

ℒlat=𝔼⁡[‖ϵG−ϵ^θ​(bt,Xt,P,t)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert\epsilon_{G}-\widehat{\epsilon}_{\theta}(b_{t},X_{t},P,t)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]. (50)

Projection is applied after every noising and reverse update. With the usual DDPM notation (Ho et al., 2020), the reverse step is

bt−1=ΠG​[1αt​(bt−1−αt1−α¯t​ϵ^θ)+σt​z],σt2=βt​1−α¯t−11−α¯t.b_{t-1}=\Pi_{G}\!\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}}\left(b_{t}-\frac{1-\alpha_{t}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\,\widehat{\epsilon}_{\theta}\right)+\sigma_{t}z\right],\qquad\sigma_{t}^{2}=\beta_{t}\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}. (51)

F.3 Anchor-coordinate score matching

Each occupied Wyckoff orbit is parameterized by one anchor coordinate. Its Wyckoff affine operators deterministically expand that anchor into the full orbit. During training, coordinate noise and denoising targets are projected onto the free anchor coordinates; during sampling, the predicted field is projected in the same way before the updated anchors are re-expanded.

Let uwn∗​(Xt,X0,σt)u_{\mathrm{wn}}^{*}(X_{t},X_{0};\sigma_{t}) denote the wrapped-normal denoising target on the fractional-coordinate torus under the adopted noise normalization, and let Π𝒜⁡(P)\Pi_{\mathcal{A}(P)} project a full-cell field to the anchor chart defined by PP. The coordinate objective is

ℒcoord=𝔼⁡[‖Π𝒜⁡(P)​(u^θ​(Xt,bt,P,t)−uwn∗​(Xt,X0,σt))‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{coord}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert\Pi_{\mathcal{A}(P)}\left(\widehat{u}_{\theta}(X_{t},b_{t},P,t)-u_{\mathrm{wn}}^{*}(X_{t},X_{0};\sigma_{t})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]. (52)

The reverse process uses a coordinate corrector followed by a joint predictor step for the lattice and coordinates. After each update, orbit expansion reconstructs the complete unit cell, so every intermediate structure obeys the generated space group.

F.4 Architecture and training settings

The geometry model is trained on the conventional-cell lattice and orbit anchors of each training structure. Table 8 lists the settings used by DynaCrys and its smaller size variant, DynaCrys-small.

Appendix G Evaluation Protocol

This appendix specifies the common evaluation chain summarized in Section 5.1. All cross-method values are computed from generated structures.

G.1 Relaxation and downstream analysis

Benchmark and generation budget.

We evaluate crystal generation on MP-20 (Xie et al., 2022). The training partition is the novelty reference and the test partition is the coverage reference. Each method contributes approximately 10,000 candidates. The fixed generation budget is 10,000 per run except for WyFormer, whose released set contains 9,999 structures.

Relaxation and stability.

Structures are relaxed without symmetry constraints. CHGNet (Deng et al., 2023) is the primary relaxation engine, and the same as-generated structures are independently re-relaxed and analyzed with MACE-MP-0 (Batatia et al., 2025). They define two separate evaluation rulers: values are compared across methods within an engine, not across engines. Energy above the convex hull is evaluated against a fixed, MP2020-corrected DFT hull snapshot from the Materials Project (Jain et al., 2013), dated 2023-02-07. We use thresholds τ∈{0,0.1}\tau\in\{0,0.1\} eV/atom and summarize the relaxed population by median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}}.

Matching and symmetry.

Structural novelty is evaluated against the MP-20 training partition and uniqueness within each generated set using pymatgen’s StructureMatcher (Ong et al., 2013) with ltol=0.2=0.2, stol=0.3=0.3, and angle_tol=5∘=5^{\circ}. Coverage uses the MP-20 test partition. Space groups are identified from the relaxed structures with spglib (Togo et al., 2024) through SpacegroupAnalyzer, using symprec=0.1=0.1 Å and angle_tolerance=5∘=5^{\circ}. SSUN counts only structures successfully identified as non-P​1P1.

G.2 Metrics and accounting

For a threshold τ\tau, RelStab@τ\tau counts relaxed structures with ehull≤τe_{\mathrm{hull}}\leq\tau, SUN@τ\tau additionally requires uniqueness and novelty, and SSUN@τ\tau further requires a non-P​1P1 space group.

For each geometry-relaxed structure, a template key comprises the re-identified space group and the multiset of occupied conventional Wyckoff rows; element labels are excluded. Template U.N. counts the distinct keys absent from the MP-20 training-template reference.

The RMSD analysis pairs each as-generated structure with its relaxed endpoint using the MatterGen-style matching protocol (Zeni et al., 2025). The main-text mean RMSD is averaged over pairs for which a structural correspondence is found; the matched percentage uses all evaluated pairs as its denominator. The CHGNet and MACE-MP-0 endpoint pairs are formed and summarized independently.

G.3 Evaluation runs and aggregation

SGEquiDiff and each reported DynaCrys configuration are evaluated over five independent sampling runs and summarized by the arithmetic mean of the per-run metrics, without pooling structures across runs. When dispersion is reported, it is the sample standard deviation of those per-run values. The other baselines are single evaluated sets.

G.4 Timing

Sampling time covers each method’s complete generation procedure through the as-generated structure. For DynaCrys, this includes both symbolic generation and symmetry-constrained geometry generation. Time per structure is elapsed generation time divided by the number of requested structures. All timed methods are measured on the same machine with one NVIDIA H100 GPU and 32 physical CPU cores. The baseline timing runs contain 2,000 structures; comparisons are restricted to methods for which this same-machine measurement is available.

G.5 Symmetry sensitivity

Table 9 applies the SSUN symmetry gate with the spglib detection tolerance symprec set to 0.010.01, 0.050.05, or 0.10.1 Å, while angle_tolerance remains fixed at 5∘5^{\circ}. Relaxed structures and their stability, uniqueness, and novelty labels remain fixed; only space-group re-identification changes. Across both evaluation rulers and stability thresholds, SSUN varies by less than one percentage point over this range, and the ordering of the three configurations is unchanged.

H.2 Space-group distribution

Table 2 summarizes the breadth of the generated space-group distribution through Eff. SGs. Figure 3 shows the corresponding distribution for the canonical DynaCrys configuration, whose samples span a broad set of space groups.

Appendix I Penalty-Inclusive RMSD

Table 11 complements the matched-pair mean in Table 3. When the common matcher does not recover a correspondence, the penalty-inclusive mean assigns that pair the finite cap used by the common MatterGen-style evaluator before averaging. The resulting quantity retains every evaluated pair while using the same as-generated structures and relaxation endpoints as the main-text RMSD comparison.

Appendix J Geometry-Step Sensitivity

To isolate the geometry schedule, we reuse the canonical DynaCrys symbolic samples and geometry checkpoint while varying only the number of reverse steps.

The moderately shortened schedule remains close to the full schedule, whereas more aggressive reductions sharply reduce SUN rates at both stability thresholds. We therefore use the full geometry reverse schedule in the reported configurations.

Appendix K Dynamic Space-Group Coupling

At each reverse step, DynaCrys predicts the clean space-group factor pθ​(G0∣xt)p_{\theta}(G_{0}\mid x_{t}) from the current symbolic state. Marginal-GG replaces this state-dependent factor with the training-set marginal at every reverse step, while the legality constraints and the remaining generation process are unchanged:

pθ​(G0∣xt)⟶πG​(G0).p_{\theta}(G_{0}\mid x_{t})\;\longrightarrow\;\pi_{G}(G_{0}). (53)

Marginal-GG lowers SUN and RelStab at both thresholds and raises median ehulle_{\mathrm{hull}} for all three configurations. This consistent degradation supports coupling the space-group update to the evolving symbolic state.
